briefFidelity: FAIL on three named requirements. (1) The brief asks for banding 'filling the frame edge to edge with no single element dominating'. Before reading it I wrote, unprompted, that 'the frame is barely used - every token is a centred island with wide empty margins on all four sides, nothing bleeds, nothing touches an edge'. All twelve are floating centred vignettes occupying roughly a quarter to a third of the canvas; even the densest (10443, 10622) leave large margins on every side. This is not a near miss, it is the inverse of the instruction, and it has a second-order cost: an island floating in a dark field reads as an object sitting on a ground, which reinstates exactly the 'ground plane' the brief forbids. A core sample is a section that runs off all four edges because the core continues past the frame; this is a specimen photographed on a black table. (2) 'No single element dominating' is broken by a primitive the brief never asks for. The brief says sediment as PURE PATTERN, 'only the section itself', yet every token carries small rotated quadrilaterals orbiting above and below the stack; in 9369 - and in the 512 hero, which is the same token - those tan squares are unambiguously the loudest thing in the picture and the actual banding is a small compressed stack squeezed between them. 10801 is quads ONLY, with no beds at all: a token in a bedding collection carrying zero bedding. (3) 'Bands should differ in thickness and weight so the eye reads a sequence rather than a texture' is met in the sparse and mid tokens and lost in the dense ones - at browse size I described 10443/10622/9727 as 'a single textured smudge', which is the failure the sentence names. Palette is the clean hit: I independently described umber, ochre, sand, cold slate over a dark base, which is the brief verbatim.
seedVariation: PASS, and it is the strongest thing here. On the 120px sheet these are twelve works, not twelve rotations. Bed count ranges from about five (9906) to forty-plus full-width lines (10443); the set splits legibly into cool slate tokens (9011, 10085, 10622, 10980) and warm ochre tokens (9548, 9727, 10443); spacing runs from even striation to clustered. They also hold a shared identity - one vocabulary, one palette, one centre-weighted stratified mass - so neither failure mode applies. The exceptions are at the sparse end: 9906 and 10801 fall out of the family rather than varying within it.
thumbnailSurvival: MIXED. The stratified silhouette and the warm/cool split survive well; ten of twelve are distinguishable at a glance. Individual hairlines do not survive - the fine striations merge, so the mid-density tokens collapse toward one shape and are separated mainly by hue and width. Two tokens fail outright at 120px: 9906 is an illegible smear and 10801 is six faint grey dots with no visible relationship to anything else in the set.
marketResponse: VISIBLE BUT INVERTED ON THE AXIS THE BRIEF NAMES. The brief: under drawdown 'the beds should thin and fewer of them survive'; in recovery 'the sequence thickens and more beds return'. Both clauses pair a thickness change with a count change. Before reading the brief I described the opposite thickness behaviour: stress 'consolidates them into fewer, thicker, heavier, higher-contrast slabs', recovery 'returns to a finer, more numerous, more dispersed striation'. Re-checked on 9011, 9369 and 9548 and it is consistent - stress is fewer AND THICKER where the brief wants fewer and thinner; recovery is more AND THINNER where the brief wants more and thicker. The count axis is right, the thickness axis is exactly backwards. Neutral-to-stress is legible at browse size; neutral-to-recovery is weak, the two states land very close on 9011 and 9369.
tokenIdentity: PASS, clearly. Each token keeps its signature across all three conditions - 9369 keeps its ring of tipped squares, 9548 keeps its compact amber block over dark brown, 9011 keeps its cool centred stack. Nothing morphs into a different object; the states read as the same specimen under different weather.
composition: This is the failure. Focal hierarchy is inverted in the quad-bearing tokens: the ornament outranks the subject. The frame is unused - a uniform centred vignette repeated twelve times, which also makes the collection monotonous at the grid level even though the individual tokens vary. No clipping, no rendering artifacts, edges are crisp at 256 and the diagonal facet crease on each square is consistent enough to read as intentional. Mush is confined to the dense tokens at 120px, and it is a consequence of cramming forty beds into a third of the canvas rather than letting them run edge to edge.
reasoning: My stage-1 description and the brief agree on palette, on the horizontal-band vocabulary and on per-token variation in bed count and spacing - three real hits, and the seed variation is genuinely good. But the description I wrote without knowing the brief contradicts the brief on the two things it states most plainly. I wrote that the frame is barely used and every token is a floating centred island with margins on all four sides; the brief demands banding that fills the frame edge to edge with no single element dominating, and the empty surround plus the orbiting squares together turn a section into an object on a ground, which is the one reading the brief explicitly rules out. And I wrote that stress thickens the beds while recovery thins them; the brief claims the reverse in both directions. A claimed transformation rendered backwards is worse than one that is invisible, because it will be described in public copy as the thing it is not, and this commitment is permanent. Competent work, coherent as a set, but it is not the thing that was asked for.
wouldChange: Let the beds run off all four edges. The stack should be a section of something that continues past the frame, not a specimen centred in a black field - that single change fixes the edge-to-edge requirement, removes the ground-plane reading, demotes the orbiting quads from dominant to incidental, and gives the dense tokens the room they need to read as a sequence instead of a smudge. Second, and cheap: flip the sign on the thickness response so drawdown thins the beds and recovery thickens them, as the brief states.
